<center> <h1>**Summary**</h1> </center>
This project aimed to predict whether a policyholder would file an insurance claim using a classification approach. After preparing and cleaning the data, I applied a variety of models, including logistic regression, LASSO, Ridge regression, and Random Forests. To address the strong class imbalance in the dataset, I performed threshold tuning and evaluated models using metrics beyond accuracy, including recall, F1 score, balanced accuracy, and AUC.
<br>

Logistic regression with backward stepwise selection and LASSO performed reasonably well when evaluated at optimized thresholds, showing modest improvements in identifying claimants. Ridge regression offered similar results, while Random Forest struggled with detecting the minority class, despite high overall accuracy. Although Boosting was considered for future work, it was not implemented due to time constraints. The project highlights the importance of appropriate metric selection, feature analysis, and threshold adjustment when dealing with imbalanced classification problems.


<center> <h1>**Purpose**</h1> </center>
The purpose of this project is to predict whether a car insurance policyholder will file a claim. Insurance companies rely on this type of prediction to assess customer risk, manage costs, and design pricing strategies. Accurately identifying which policyholders are more likely to file a claim allows insurers to take proactive steps, such as adjusting policy terms or offering discounts to low-risk drivers. This analysis explores how well statistical learning methods can classify claim behavior based on vehicle characteristics, policyholder demographics, and safety features. It also highlights the challenges with modeling imbalanced data and underlines the importance of choosing evaluation metrics suited to real-world applications.
<br>

Questions that this project aim to answer are:

- What are the most important features that influence the likelihood of a policyholder filing a claim?
- How do different modeling techniques compare in their ability to classify claim vs. no-claim policyholders?
<br>

\* Note: The "segment" variable in the dataset is used to classify vehicles based on characteristics such as size, body type, and market positioning. Segments such as A, B1, B2, C1, C2, and Utility represent different vehicle classes defined by factors like car size, price, comfort level, and performance.

- Segment A (Mini cars): Small-sized vehicles primarily designed for city commuting, fuel efficiency, and ease of parking
- Segment B (Hatchback): Slightly larger than mini cars.
  - B1: Lower sub-segment—basic subcompact models
  - B2: Upper sub-segment—higher-end, more feature-rich subcompact models
- Segment C (Medium/compact cars): These family-oriented vehicles provide enhanced comfort, space, and features, distinguishing them from B-segment cars.
  - C1: Basic compact car variants.
  - C2: Premium compact variants offering enhanced features, safety, and comfort.
- Utility Segment: Includes SUVs, crossovers, pickup trucks, or utility-focused models designed for versatility and off-road capability.

Below the correlation heatmap shows that most numeric variables in the dataset are weakly related. The strongest relationship is between policy_tenure and age_of_car, but even that is weak (around 0.17). This means that customers with longer policies tend to have slightly older cars.

There's almost no correlation between age_of_policyholder or make and whether someone files a claim (is_claim), suggesting that no single numeric variable is a strong predictor. Instead, we'll likely need to use more flexible models—like decision trees or bagging model—that can capture more complex patterns.
```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}

corrplot2 <- function(data,
                      method = "pearson",
                      sig.level = 0.05,
                      order = "original",
                      diag = FALSE,
                      type = "upper",
                      tl.srt = 90,
                      number.font = 1,
                      number.cex = 1,
                      mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0)) {
  
  data_incomplete <- data
  data <- data[complete.cases(data), ]
  mat <- cor(data, method = method)
  
  cor.mtest <- function(mat, method) {
    mat <- as.matrix(mat)
    n <- ncol(mat)
    p.mat <- matrix(NA, n, n)
    diag(p.mat) <- 0
    for (i in 1:(n - 1)) {
      for (j in (i + 1):n) {
        tmp <- cor.test(mat[, i], mat[, j], method = method)
        p.mat[i, j] <- p.mat[j, i] <- tmp$p.value
      }
    }
    colnames(p.mat) <- rownames(p.mat) <- colnames(mat)
    p.mat
  }

  p.mat <- cor.mtest(data, method = method)
  col <- colorRampPalette(c("#BB4444", "#EE9988", "#FFFFFF", "#77AADD", "#4477AA"))

  corrplot(mat, method = "color", col = col(200),
           number.font = number.font,
           mar = mar, number.cex = number.cex,
           type = type, order = order,
           addCoef.col = "black",
           tl.col = "black", tl.srt = tl.srt,
           p.mat = p.mat, sig.level = sig.level, insig = "blank",
           diag = diag)
}

# Use "eda_train" instead of "train"
numeric_vars <- train[, c("policy_tenure", "age_of_car", "age_of_policyholder", 
                              "population_density", "displacement", "cylinder", 
                              "airbags", "ncap_rating", "is_claim")]

numeric_vars <- data.frame(lapply(numeric_vars, function(x) as.numeric(as.character(x))))
corrplot2(numeric_vars)




```


<br>

After reviewing all the visualizations, summary tables, and correlation heatmaps, I have determined which variables to keep in my predictive model and which ones to remove. My goal is to keep variables that show enough variation, offer meaningful predictive importance, and make sense in the context of insurance claims, while cutting out those that are redundant, imbalanced, or lack insight.
<br>

I’ve decided to keep numerical features like **age_of_car**, **policy_tenure**, **population_density**, **airbags**, **displacement**, **cylinder**, and **ncap_rating**. Although the correlation heatmap shows no strong linear relationship with **is_claim**, these features capture important aspects of vehicle safety, usage, and risk exposure. For example, features like **airbags** and **ncap_rating** are directly tied to crash protection, which can influence claim likelihood—especially in models like decision trees that can pick up on non-linear interactions. Similarly, **population_density** can reflect traffic conditions and accident risk, even if the correlation appears weak at first glance.
<br>

On the other hand, I’m planning to drop features that have extremely skewed distributions or small variability, like **is_speed_alert**, **is_power_steering**, **is_central_locking**, and **is_power_door_locks**. Almost every vehicle includes these features, so they won’t help the model differentiate between those who file claims and those who don’t. I am also removing variables like make, model, and steering_type; they are too specific and sparsely represented across the data, which could lead to overfitting. Features like **rear_brakes_type** and **transmission_type** also fall into this category—they don’t offer much variation and are likely already captured by more detailed specs.
<br>

Lastly, while variables like **fuel_type**, **gear_box**, and **engine_type** bring some variety, they tend to cluster around just a few common categories. Because of that, they often overlap with more descriptive features like **displacement** or **max_power**. To keep things simple and to enhance clarity, I will focus on the variables that provide broader, more continuous understanding and eliminate the overly granular ones. Overall, I’m focused on a set of predictors that emphasize safety, vehicle complexity, and environmental exposure—without weighing the model down with noise.
<br>


<center> <h1>**Methodology**</h1> </center>
To predict whether a policyholder will file an insurance claim, I structured the problem as a supervised classification task because the outcome variable, is_claim, is binary, meaning it can take only two values. This way lets for the application of various classification algorithms to predict the likelihood of a policyholder filing a claim and enables a thorough analysis of the factors influencing claim behavior. I selected diverse models to handle the specific challenges of insurance claim prediction, balancing interpretability, regularization, flexibility, and predictive power. These include Logistic Regression for baseline predictions, LASSO and Ridge Regression to handle potential multicollinearity in insurance variables, and more complex models like Random Forests and Boosting to capture non-linear relationships between policyholder characteristics and claim likelihood.
<br>

Logistic Regression serves as a foundational model, offering interpretable and explainable results through its coefficients. It assumes linearity between features and the output, but helps establish a baseline for comparison. LASSO Regression enhances this model by applying L1 regularization. This technique helps prevent overfitting and automatically removes unimportant variables, making it well-suited for high-dimensional datasets with potentially redundant features. Ridge Regression uses L2 regularization, which is appropriate for multicollinearity and balances model complexity with overfitting without excluding predictors.
<br>

I included tree-based methods to model more complex relationships and non-linear interactions. Random Forests reduce overfitting and offer better accuracy and robustness, particularly useful when variable interactions are present. Boosting methods further enhance predictive performance by sequentially learning from previous errors, adapting them for identifying subtle, complex patterns in the data.
<br>

I will evaluate each model using accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and the AUC-ROC curve to address class imbalance. I will apply K-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning and to ensure model generalizability. I will use backward stepwise selection for feature selection in Logistic Regression, implement regularization in LASSO, and rank variable importance from tree-based models. This multi-model methodology guarantees that I can compare performance across interpretable linear models and more flexible ensemble models

<br>
<center> <h1>**Results**</h1> </center>

### **Logistic Regression Model**

The logistic regression model provided insights into how different features relate to the likelihood of a policyholder filing a claim, identifying key predictors that significantly influence claim behavior. It highlighted several statistically significant variables, including age_of_car, policy_tenure, population_density, displacement, cylinder, and ncap_rating. Notably, age_of_car had a strong negative coefficient, indicating that newer vehicles are more likely to be involved in claims. In contrast, some predictors, such as airbags, is_esc, and is_tpms, showed no statistical significance.
<br>

Upon reviewing the model's performance, I realized that relying only on the typical accuracy metric would not provide an accurate evaluation. Even with great accuracy of 93.6% across various thresholds, this figure was somewhat misleading, as the model predominantly predicted non-claims due to the significant class imbalance. To gain a better idea of the model's effectiveness, I experimented with different classification thresholds ranging from 0.1 to 0.9. Throughout this process, I focused on essential metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, precision, recall, F1 score, and AUC to evaluate its true performance.
<br>

The best trade-off between sensitivity and specificity appeared at a lower threshold of 0.1. At this point, the model's accuracy dropped slightly to 87.3%, but its specificity improved to 11.7% while maintaining a sensitivity of 92.4%. Most importantly, this threshold delivered the highest balanced accuracy (0.521), indicating a better balance between detecting true positives and true negatives. The precision (0.9388) and F1 score (0.9315) were also strongest at this threshold, indicating that the model was more reliable in predicting actual claimants. While the AUC of 0.6121 indicates modest predictive power, it still shows that the model performs better..  

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# 1. DATA PREPARATION


# Define predictors to keep
selected_predictors <- c("age_of_car", "policy_tenure", "population_density",
                         "airbags", "displacement", "cylinder", "ncap_rating",
                         "is_esc", "is_tpms", "is_parking_camera", "is_brake_assist")

# Stratified sampling
set.seed(123)
split_index <- createDataPartition(train$is_claim, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_split <- train[split_index, ]
test_split  <- train[-split_index, ]

# Create clean datasets
train_clean <- train_split[, c("is_claim", selected_predictors)]
test_clean  <- test_split[, selected_predictors]

# Convert binary features safely
binary_vars <- c("is_esc", "is_tpms", "is_parking_camera", "is_brake_assist")
convert_binary <- function(x) ifelse(x == "Yes", 1, ifelse(x == "No", 0, NA))
train_clean[binary_vars] <- lapply(train_split[binary_vars], convert_binary)
test_clean[binary_vars]  <- lapply(test_split[binary_vars], convert_binary)

# Convert other variables to numeric
vars_to_numeric <- c("airbags", "displacement", "cylinder", "ncap_rating")
convert_clean_numeric <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(x)))
train_clean[vars_to_numeric] <- lapply(train_clean[vars_to_numeric], convert_clean_numeric)
test_clean[vars_to_numeric]  <- lapply(test_clean[vars_to_numeric], convert_clean_numeric)

# Convert outcome to factor
train_clean$is_claim <- as.factor(train_clean$is_claim)
```


```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# 2. FIT LOGISTIC MODEL


logit_model <- glm(is_claim ~ ., data = train_clean, family = "binomial")

# Predict probabilities on test set
logit_probs <- predict(logit_model, newdata = test_clean, type = "response")

# Remove NAs
valid_idx <- !is.na(logit_probs)
logit_probs <- logit_probs[valid_idx]
test_actual <- factor(test_split$is_claim[valid_idx], levels = c(0, 1))

summary(logit_model)

```


```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# 3. THRESHOLD LOOP


thresholds <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)
results_list <- list()

for (t in thresholds) {
  logit_pred <- factor(ifelse(logit_probs > t, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
  cm <- confusionMatrix(logit_pred, test_actual)
  
  acc <- cm$overall["Accuracy"]
  recall <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  spec <- cm$byClass["Specificity"]
  prec <- cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]
  f1 <- 2 * (prec * recall) / (prec + recall)
  bal_acc <- cm$byClass["Balanced Accuracy"]
  auc_val <- auc(test_actual, logit_probs)
  
  results_list[[as.character(t)]] <- c(
    Threshold = t,
    Accuracy = acc,
    Recall = recall,
    Specificity = spec,
    Precision = prec,
    F1 = f1,
    Balanced_Accuracy = bal_acc,
    AUC = auc_val
  )
}

# Convert list to data frame and view
threshold_summary <- do.call(rbind, results_list) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric),
         across(everything(), round, 4))

# View summary table
print(threshold_summary)

```

### **Logistic Regression with Backward Stepwise Selected Features**

Using backward stepwise selection, I refined the logistic regression model to include only the most relevant predictors. This reduced the model's complexity while preserving key information. I then evaluated its performance across different classification thresholds from 0.1 to 0.9. The best-performing threshold was 0.1, where the model achieved a balanced accuracy of 52.0%, a recall of 92.4%, and a precision of 9.4%, into an F1 Score of 10.3%. While the accuracy was slightly lower at this threshold (87.3%) compared to higher thresholds (which consistently reached 93.6%), this setting offered a better trade-off between detecting actual claimants and avoiding false alarms.
```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# 1. Backward stepwise selection
step_model <- step(glm(is_claim ~ ., data = train_clean, family = binomial),
                   direction = "backward", trace = 0)

# 2. Predict probabilities using the selected model
step_probs <- predict(step_model, newdata = test_clean, type = "response")
test_actual <- factor(test_split$is_claim, levels = c(0, 1))  # ensure factor

# 3. Define threshold 
thresholds <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)
results_list <- list()

# 4. Evaluate performance across thresholds
for (t in thresholds) {
  step_pred <- factor(ifelse(step_probs > t, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
  cm <- confusionMatrix(step_pred, test_actual, positive = "1")

  precision <- cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]
  recall <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]

  # Avoid NaN from 0/0 by checking denominator
  if (is.na(precision) || is.na(recall) || (precision + recall == 0)) {
    f1 <- 0
  } else {
    f1 <- 2 * ((precision * recall) / (precision + recall))
  }

  results_list[[as.character(t)]] <- c(
    Threshold = t,
    Accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    Recall = recall,
    Specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    Precision = precision,
    F1 = f1,
    Balanced_Accuracy = cm$byClass["Balanced Accuracy"],
    AUC = auc(test_actual, step_probs)
  )
}

# 5. Summary table
stepwise_threshold_summary <- do.call(rbind, results_list) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), round, 4))

# 6. Final results
print(stepwise_threshold_summary)

# 7. Confusion Matrix at best threshold based on Balanced Accuracy
best_row <- stepwise_threshold_summary[which.max(stepwise_threshold_summary$Balanced_Accuracy), ]
best_threshold <- best_row$Threshold

cat("Best threshold based on Balanced Accuracy:", best_threshold, "\n")
final_pred <- factor(ifelse(step_probs > best_threshold, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(final_pred, test_actual)
print(conf_matrix)

# 8. ROC Curve
roc_obj <- roc(test_actual, step_probs, quiet = TRUE)
plot(roc_obj, main = paste("ROC Curve (Threshold =", best_threshold, ")"), col = "darkorange")
text(0.6, 0.2, labels = paste("AUC =", round(auc(roc_obj), 4)), col = "black", cex = 1.2)

# View the formula of the final selected model
#final_formula <- formula(step_model)
#print(final_formula)

```
The logistic regression model using backward stepwise selection below identifies several statistically significant predictors of whether a policyholder will file a claim. Policy_tenure has a highly significant and positive coefficient, indicating that long-standing customers are more likely to file a claim. This may seem counterintuitive but could reflect factors such as increased vehicle usage or a greater likelihood of claim awareness over time.
<br>

Age_of_car and population_density both have significant negative coefficients, suggesting that policyholders with newer vehicles and those living in more densely populated areas are less likely to file claims. The last could be due to urban drivers potentially covering shorter distances or having better access to public transport.
<br>

In terms of vehicle specifications, displacement is negatively associated with claims, meaning vehicles with larger engine displacement are slightly less likely to be involved in claims. Cylinder count, on the other hand, has a positive and statistically significant coefficient, implying that cars with more cylinders may possess a higher risk, perhaps due to being more performance-oriented or driven differently. Other variables like ncap_rating, airbags, and is_brake_assist demonstrate weaker significance levels but may still provide predictive value and should be considered alongside other features or tested in further models.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
summary(step_model)

```

### **LASSO Logistic Regression**
Based on the outputs from the LASSO regression model below, similar performance patterns emerge as observed in the previous logistic regression models. The model's AUC of 0.6114 indicates that it performs better than random guessing when distinguishing between claimants and non-claimants. At the optimal threshold of 0.1, LASSO achieved an accuracy of 88.2%, sensitivity of 93.5%, and specificity of 11.1%. The high sensitivity reveals that the model effectively identifies most non-claimants, who dominate the dataset, but struggles to identify true claimants (specificity) due to its low performance.
<br>

The precision and F1 score at this threshold—0.9390 and 0.1074 respectively—indicate that while the model makes a meaningful number of correct positive predictions, the low F1 score reflects the difficulties presented by the imbalance in class representation. At higher thresholds (0.2 and beyond), LASSO fails to identify any claimants, resulting in NaN values for precision and F1. This outcome stems from the model predicts all observations as non-claimants As with logistic regression, threshold adjustment was essential to enhance the model’s usefulness, especially in identifying the minority class. LASSO’s advantage is its automatic feature selection via regularization, which controls overfitting and improves generalizability, but it still struggles with class imbalance.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}

# 1. 
x_train <- model.matrix(is_claim ~ ., data = train_clean)[, -1]
y_train <- as.numeric(as.character(train_clean$is_claim))
x_test  <- model.matrix(~ ., data = test_clean)[, -1]
test_actual <- factor(test_split$is_claim, levels = c(0, 1))

# 2. Cross-validation for lambda
set.seed(123)
cv_lasso <- cv.glmnet(x_train, y_train, family = "binomial", alpha = 1)
best_lambda <- cv_lasso$lambda.min

# 3. 
lasso_model <- glmnet(x_train, y_train, family = "binomial", alpha = 1, lambda = best_lambda)
lasso_probs <- predict(lasso_model, newx = x_test, type = "response")

# 4. Threshold evaluation
thresholds <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)
results_list <- list()

for (t in thresholds) {
  lasso_pred <- factor(ifelse(lasso_probs > t, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
  cm <- confusionMatrix(lasso_pred, test_actual, positive = "1")

  precision <- cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]
  recall <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  f1 <- ifelse((precision + recall) == 0, NA, 2 * ((precision * recall) / (precision + recall)))

  results_list[[as.character(t)]] <- c(
    Threshold = t,
    Accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    Recall = recall,
    Specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    Precision = precision,
    F1 = f1,
    Balanced_Accuracy = cm$byClass["Balanced Accuracy"],
    AUC = auc(test_actual, as.numeric(lasso_probs))
  )
}

# 5. Summary Table
lasso_threshold_summary <- do.call(rbind, results_list) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), round, 4))

print(lasso_threshold_summary)

# 6. Confusion Matrix at Best Threshold
best_row <- lasso_threshold_summary[which.max(lasso_threshold_summary$Balanced_Accuracy), ]
best_threshold <- best_row$Threshold
cat("Best threshold based on Balanced Accuracy:", best_threshold, "\n")

final_pred <- factor(ifelse(lasso_probs > best_threshold, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(final_pred, test_actual)
print(conf_matrix)

# 7. ROC Curve
roc_obj <- roc(test_actual, as.numeric(lasso_probs), quiet = TRUE)
plot(roc_obj, main = paste("LASSO Regression ROC Curve (Threshold =", best_threshold, ")"), col = "darkgreen")
text(0.6, 0.2, labels = paste("AUC =", round(auc(roc_obj), 4)), col = "black", cex = 1.2)

```
<br>


### **Ridge Regression with Backward Stepwise Selected Features**
The Ridge Regression model, evaluated at a classification threshold of 0.1, performs reasonably well given the class imbalance in the dataset, where only about 6% of policyholders filed a claim. The model's overall accuracy of 88.15% is largely due to its strong ability to identify non-claimants. This is evident in the high sensitivity (93.44%), showing that the model correctly flags most non-claim cases. However, its specificity remains low at 10.81%, meaning it struggles to correctly identify non-claimants. Despite this, the precision is high (93.88%), indicating that when the model predicts a claim, it is likely to be correct. The balanced accuracy of 52.13% and an AUC of 0.6111 suggest that the model performs moderately well.

<br>

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
# 1. Use only the features selected by backward stepwise
selected_vars <- c("age_of_car", "policy_tenure", "population_density",
                   "airbags", "displacement", "cylinder", "ncap_rating", "is_brake_assist")

# 2. Create matrices
x_train_ridge <- model.matrix(as.formula(paste("~", paste(selected_vars, collapse = " + "))),
                              data = train_clean)[, -1]
y_train_ridge <- as.numeric(as.character(train_clean$is_claim))
x_test_ridge <- model.matrix(as.formula(paste("~", paste(selected_vars, collapse = " + "))),
                             data = test_clean)[, -1]
test_actual <- factor(test_split$is_claim, levels = c(0, 1))

# 3. Fit Ridge Regression with Cross-Validation
set.seed(123)
cv_ridge <- cv.glmnet(x_train_ridge, y_train_ridge, family = "binomial", alpha = 0)
best_lambda_ridge <- cv_ridge$lambda.min

# 4. Final model and probability predictions
ridge_model <- glmnet(x_train_ridge, y_train_ridge, family = "binomial", alpha = 0, lambda = best_lambda_ridge)
ridge_probs <- as.numeric(predict(ridge_model, newx = x_test_ridge, type = "response")) # Had an error, so I used as.numeric

# 5. Threshold tuning loop
thresholds <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)
results_list <- list()

for (t in thresholds) {
  ridge_pred <- factor(ifelse(ridge_probs > t, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
  cm <- confusionMatrix(ridge_pred, test_actual, positive = "1")

  precision <- cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]
  recall <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  f1 <- ifelse(is.na(precision) | is.na(recall), NA, 2 * ((precision * recall) / (precision + recall)))

  results_list[[as.character(t)]] <- c(
    Threshold = t,
    Accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    Recall = recall,
    Specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    Precision = precision,
    F1 = f1,
    Balanced_Accuracy = cm$byClass["Balanced Accuracy"],
    AUC = auc(test_actual, ridge_probs)
  )
}

# 6. Combine and format results
ridge_threshold_summary <- do.call(rbind, results_list) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), round, 4))

# 7. Best threshold evaluation
best_row <- ridge_threshold_summary[which.max(ridge_threshold_summary$Balanced_Accuracy), ]
best_threshold <- best_row$Threshold

cat("Best threshold based on Balanced Accuracy:", best_threshold, "\n")

final_pred <- factor(ifelse(ridge_probs > best_threshold, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(final_pred, test_actual)
print(conf_matrix)

# 8. ROC Curve
roc_obj <- roc(test_actual, ridge_probs, quiet = TRUE)
plot(roc_obj, main = paste("Ridge Regression ROC Curve (Threshold =", best_threshold, ")"), col = "purple")
text(x = 0.6, y = 0.2, labels = paste("AUC =", round(auc(roc_obj), 4)), col = "black", cex = 1.2)

```
<br>


### **Random Forest**
Despite achieving a high overall accuracy of 93.3%, the Random Forest model struggles to detect actual claims due to its low sensitivity. With a sensitivity of just 0.0067, the model correctly identified fewer than 1% of claimants. On the other hand, the specificity was 0.996, reflecting strong performance in identifying non-claimants. However, due to the imbalance in the dataset, this leads to a distorted picture of performance. The balanced accuracy, which averages sensitivity and specificity, was only 0.501, underscoring the model’s difficulty in handling the minority class.
<br>

The AUC of 0.511 further supports this finding, indicating the model’s inability to separate claimants from non-claimants. Additionally, at higher thresholds, most precision and F1 score values returned as NaN, which occurs when no positive cases are predicted rendering those metrics undefined. These outcomes emphasize that while the model appears effective in aggregate terms, it performs poorly when the focus shifts to detecting actual claims.
```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}

# 1. Fit Random Forest model
set.seed(123)
rf_model <- randomForest(as.factor(is_claim) ~ ., data = train_clean, ntree = 500)

# 2. Predict probabilities on test set
rf_probs <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test_clean, type = "prob")[, 2]
test_actual <- factor(test_split$is_claim, levels = c(0, 1))

# 3. Evaluate across thresholds
thresholds <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.1)
results_list <- list()

for (t in thresholds) {
  rf_pred <- factor(ifelse(rf_probs > t, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
  cm <- confusionMatrix(rf_pred, test_actual, positive = "1")
  
  precision <- cm$byClass["Pos Pred Value"]
  recall <- cm$byClass["Sensitivity"]
  f1 <- ifelse((precision + recall) == 0, NA, 2 * ((precision * recall) / (precision + recall)))
  
  results_list[[as.character(t)]] <- c(
    Threshold = t,
    Accuracy = cm$overall["Accuracy"],
    Recall = recall,
    Specificity = cm$byClass["Specificity"],
    Precision = precision,
    F1 = f1,
    Balanced_Accuracy = cm$byClass["Balanced Accuracy"],
    AUC = auc(test_actual, rf_probs)
  )
}

# 4. Summary table
rf_results <- do.call(rbind, results_list) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), round, 4))

print(rf_results)

# 5. Confusion Matrix
best_threshold <- rf_results$Threshold[which.max(rf_results$Balanced_Accuracy)]
cat("Best threshold based on Balanced Accuracy:", best_threshold, "\n")

rf_final_pred <- factor(ifelse(rf_probs > best_threshold, 1, 0), levels = c(0, 1))
conf_matrix <- confusionMatrix(rf_final_pred, test_actual, positive = "1")
print(conf_matrix)

# 6. ROC Curve
roc_obj <- roc(test_actual, rf_probs, quiet = TRUE)
plot(roc_obj, main = paste("Random Forest ROC Curve (Threshold =", best_threshold, ")"), col = "darkgreen")
text(0.6, 0.2, labels = paste("AUC =", round(auc(roc_obj), 4)), col = "black", cex = 1.2)

```

A variable importance plot was developed to provide deeper insights into each predictor's impact. According to the Mean Decrease in Gini, policy_tenure stood out as the most significant variable, followed by age_of_car and population_density. These findings confirm earlier models, strengthening the hypothesis that experience, vehicle age, and regional factors significantly influence claim risk.

```{r, message=FALSE, echo = FALSE}
importance(rf_model)
```

<center> <h1>**Conclusions**</h1> </center>
Across multiple models, policy_tenure, age_of_car, and population_density consistently emerged as top predictors of claim likelihood. Logistic regression and LASSO performed well, achieving high sensitivity and balanced accuracy when thresholds were optimized. However, tree-based models like Random Forest underperformed in this imbalanced classification task, likely due to difficulty identifying claimants. These results highlight the importance of threshold tuning, feature selection, and choosing evaluation metrics, as they significantly impacted the model's ability to accurately predict a policyholder would claim. While boosting was not implemented due to time constraints, it remains a potential path for future work. Given its ability to sequentially learn from misclassified observations, it may offer modest improvements in detecting claimants. However, due to the extreme class imbalance in the data, even Boosting may face challenges in significantly improving prediction accuracy without additional resampling or cost-sensitive adjustments.
<br>
<br>

<center> <h1>**Discussion**</h1> </center>

This project presented a combination of challenges and learning experinces. One of the most difficult aspects was the data preparation, especially the challenges encountered in encoding and factoring certain variables. Many features initially returned NaN values during modeling, which led to days of troubleshooting. In the end, I restarted the process entirely, which was necessary to address the persistent issues and ultimately helped me clean and structure the data more effectively. Additionally, understanding the automotive context of many variables proved time consuming. I spent significant time researching what terms like displacement, ncap_rating, and cylinder meant and how they related to vehicle safety or performance.
<br>

I enjoyed validating my model outputs. At one point, I worried that I had misapplied modeling techniques, but through exploration and evaluation, I realized that the real challenge stemmed from the class imbalance in the dataset—not a modeling error. This deepened my appreciation for metrics like recall, F1 score, and balanced accuracy. Given more time, I would have explored more advanced ensemble techniques like XGBoost and Gradient Boosting, or compared results with a Support Vector Machine to determine if these methods could handle the class imbalance more effectively.
